sentences.text: From analysis to the client report: effect sizes, figures, and honest reporting of a multimodal ad study
This workshop starts where a data set is ready and a client has asked, "Which ad should we run?"
It ends with two finished products, an academic results and discussion section and a client report, both honest about what the data can and cannot show.
Every section explains why before how.
Analysis and reporting is four jobs.
Write the questions and their tests down before you see the numbers: the analysis plan.

Look at the data in iMotions Lab 11 point 1, whose Aggregate Replay, heatmaps, scan paths, A O I metrics, Reports, and Dashboard are for seeing and showing; the numbers for tests come from the exports.

Test each question in R or Excel, giving every result an effect size, a number that says how large a difference or relation is, and a 95 percent confidence interval (confidence interval), the range of values the data are compatible with, and draw figures that show every participant.
Then write it up twice:

A P A results and discussion: every planned test with its statistic, degrees of freedom, p value, effect size, and confidence interval, as a marketing journal expects, then what the results mean and do not mean.
Client report: the same results in plain business language, one finding per page, with the uncertainty said in words and a recommendation that follows from the data.

The worked example continues the simulated Multimodal Ad Study of Workshop 7: 24 participants (P 01 to P 24), 22 in the analysis sample, watched two 30 seconds ads for the invented water bottle brands Altavo and Brenlow while a Smart Eye Aurora tracked their gaze, Affectiva aff decks scored their faces, and a Shimmer 3 G S R plus recorded skin conductance (G S R); then they answered a survey.
Workshop 8 runs the three Workshop 7 hypotheses, H 1 to H 3, again on the same analysis ready files, gets exactly the same numbers, and adds the analysis a client project needs.
If you skipped Workshop 7, section 03 recaps the study on one page and the data folder holds its files.
No person was recorded.
Time needed.
About 5 hours over two sittings: sections 01 to 05 (planning and the iMotions tools) in the first, 06 to 10 (statistics and the two write ups) in the second
Equipment.
A lab computer with iMotions Lab 11 point 1 for the visual tools (sections 04 and 05); any computer with R and RStudio, or Excel 365, for the rest
SoftwareiMotions Lab 11 point 1; R 4.3 with read R, D plier, tidy R, G G plot 2, L M E 4, and L M E R test; Excel 365 (the version on the lab computers is still to be verified)

Data filesanalysis full dot R and its console log analysis output dot T X T, the analysis plan, every test, the Excel workbook, the model results text and client report, and the five Workshop 7 inputs; start with the read me
How to use.
Work top to bottom, answer each quick check, then tick the section
You need this page and, for sections 04 and 05, a lab computer with iMotions Lab 11 point 1.
The statistics stay at the level of a first course, and sections 07 and 08 offer an R route and an Excel route that assume no programming.
Terms with a dotted underline open a definition when you tap them; help center links open after you sign in through my dot imotions dot com (start with Analysis Overview).
Practice the iMotions steps only on the vendor demonstration studies in the Library, never on a lab study with participants, and refer to the vendor sample reports by their titles only.
The rule this workshop keeps repeating Report every planned test, significant or not.
Write the questions and their tests before you see the numbers, give every result an effect size and a confidence interval, and keep what the data show apart from what the client hopes they show.

"Not significant" does not mean "no difference": with 22 participants (simulated), only large effects could be detected, so for a small difference between the ads the honest sentence is "we cannot tell" (Greenland and colleagues

Say what analysis and reporting covers, name the two written products and how they differ, place the worked example after Workshop 7, and state the rule that every planned test is reported with an effect size and a confidence interval, significant or not.
From questions to an analysis plan

The fictional client of the worked example, the Altavo brand team, wants to know how its new hiking ad performs against a competitor's cycling ad, and in the end it asks one question: which ad should we run?
That is a decision, not a research question.
No single test can answer it, because "better" can mean seen, felt, liked, or remembered, and each of these is measured by a different sensor, on a different scale, with a different test.
The first job of analysis is translation, from the client's question to research questions that each name a measure, a comparison, and a test.
The model client report (client report model dot M D) lists what the team wanted to know: "Do viewers look at the brand?
Does the ad produce positive emotion?
Does it get a physical reaction?
Do viewers like it?
Do they remember the brand?"
The team also asked about purchase intention.
Each becomes a research question with a measure:
Look at the brand: gaze dwell time on the Logo, Product, and Headline A O I's, as a percent of the 30 seconds ad (eye tracking).
Positive emotion: the percent of time with aff decks Joy at or above 50, with Engagement and Brow Furrow beside it (facial expression).
Physical reaction: G S R Peaks Per Minute during each ad and during the Baseline, a gray screen shown before the ads (skin conductance).
Liking: liking of each ad from 1 to 7 (survey).
Memory: brand recall for each ad, correct or not (survey).
Purchase intention: one item from 1 to 7, asked once after both ads, about reusable water bottles in general.
It names no brand, so it cannot compare the ads, and the plan says so instead of forcing a test.

Translation also brings up questions the client did not ask but the analysis must: did the order of the ads matter (a check of the counterbalancing), how do the measures of different sensors go together across people, and how many viewers would the next study need?
An analysis plan has one row per question and makes five decisions in each row: the question, the measures, the test, the correction for multiple tests, and the status.
The worked example's plan, simulated analysis plan dot C S V (simulated), has eleven rows; the table below condenses it.
Section 02 explains each test in plain words, so for now read the table for its structure.
Read the table by its columns.
Each question can be answered with a yes or no, or with an estimate.
Each measure names the export it comes from.
Each test is chosen before the data are seen, often with a check beside it: a second analysis that relaxes one assumption of the first, such as a Wilcoxon test beside a t test.
If the check disagrees, the report says so.
The correction column names the family of tests and the method.
The status column says when the row was written.
Status is where honesty starts.
A planned analysis was written down before the results were seen.
H 1 to H 3 were written into the study protocol before any participant was recorded.

Q 4 to Q 6 and the order check O 1 were written into the plan after the data existed but before these analyses were run, so they carry less confirmatory weight than H 1 to H 3, and the analysis strategy of the model write up (results text dot M D, part a) says so in one sentence.
E1 is an exploratory analysis, labeled as such in advance: it estimates 21 correlations, reports each with an interval and without a p value, and tests nothing.
P 1 is not a test at all; it asks what the design could detect.

A test run at alpha equals point 0 5, the false positive rate the researcher agrees to accept, has a 5 percent chance of a false positive when nothing is going on, so a report with many tests will contain some "significant" results that chance alone produced.
E1 makes the point with arithmetic: if none of its seven measures were related to any other, about 1.05 of its 21 intervals (21 times point 0 5) would still exclude zero.

The iMotions article General Data Analysis and Interpretation says it in the vendor's words: "The more tests we conduct, the higher the chance of observing a false-positive result," which is why it recommends "a clear research question, a hypothesis, and an analysis plan before data collection so that we do as few comparisons as possible."
A family of tests is the set of tests that together answer one question.
Within each family the plan applies Holm's correction, which keeps the chance of at least one false positive in the family at point 0 5; section 06 shows how it works.

Families follow the questions, not convenience: H 3 is a family of two tests, one per ad; the six A O I comparisons of Q 4 a form another; Q 5 holds three expressions, Q 6 the three comparisons the client asked for, and O 1 eight order checks.
H 1 and H 2 are each a family of one, with their per ad estimates as checks.
The omnibus tests of Q 4 , single F tests of whether any of several means differ, are not adjusted.
Draw the families before the results exist: moving a test into a smaller family after seeing its p value is one more way to make a result look stronger than it is.
A plan written after the results is a story, not a plan.
Once you know which comparison came out significant, it is easy, and usually unintended, to tell the analysis as if that comparison had been the question all along.
Kerr named this harking, hypothesizing after the results are known.
Undisclosed flexibility in which measures, exclusions, and tests to report allows presenting almost anything as significant.
Preregistration, a dated plan written before the data exist, separates prediction, which tests a hypothesis, from postdiction, which generates one.
Purely confirmatory research fixes the analysis in advance so that its p values mean what they claim, and exploratory work stays welcome as long as it is labeled as exploratory.
The A P A reporting standards ask authors to describe their analytic strategy separately for primary, secondary, and exploratory hypotheses, which is what the status column records.
None of this forbids looking at the data.
It forbids pretending that you had not.
In the model results the 21 exploratory correlations of E1 are reported in full, with their intervals, and "offered as hypotheses for a new study, not as findings."
The iMotions Study Template for TV and Digital Ad Testing is a one page method sheet (figures below).

It lists four "Potential Business Objectives", the modalities (G S R, E E G, eye tracking, facial expression analysis, and self report), "Sample Specs" ("N equals 30 per cell"; "Up to 3 videos per person; up to 9 masking videos"), a methodology in three steps (setup and calibration, the target videos shown in a clutter reel or within a longer viewing experience, and a brief survey of "video recall, likeability, etc.")
, and three "Key Deliverables": a time course of emotional response, visual attention heat maps, and percent time of facial expressions.
It gives no metric names, no analysis steps, and no statistics.
Two lessons follow for the plan.
First, its objectives are business objectives, like the client's question: "Understand which, of multiple, creatives may perform best in-market" still has to be translated into measures and tests.

Second, "N equals 30 per cell", where a cell is one condition, is a vendor convention, not a power calculation; the lab's study type guide (Project doc 01) treats sample sizes as "lab planning conventions, not iMotions rules" and plans 25 to 30 usable participants per condition for a screen based video test.

The worked example, with 22 participants (simulated) who each saw both ads, falls below that convention; the sensitivity analysis P 1 (section 06) says what 22 could detect and how many the next study needs.
The vendor's sample client reports open the same way, with a "Background and Objectives" slide.
The Food Testing sample report lists three numbered questions (figure below).

Read as a plan, they fall short: none names a measure or a test; the second asks how consumers respond "consciously and non-consciously" without saying how either is measured; and the third, which sample participants prefer, is the client's decision question again.
With 10 participants and only means on its charts, the report still recommends removing two of the four samples from consideration.
A plan that wrote each question with its measure and test would have forced the question of whether 10 people could settle it.

Translate a client's question into research questions with measures and tests, write the analysis plan as a table with families, corrections, and status, tell planned from exploratory analyses and say why the plan comes first, and read the vendor's ad testing template as a starting point rather than a plan.
Choosing the analysis
Three facts about a question pick its test: what is compared, what kind of number the outcome is, and how the observations are linked.
Get the third wrong and the p value is wrong, however carefully you compute it.
What is compared?
Two conditions (an ad against the Baseline, Ad A against Ad B), more than two (three A O I's), or two measures that may go together (Joy and liking).
What kind of number is the outcome?

A measured amount, such as Peaks Per Minute or dwell; a rating from 1 to 7, which is ordinal; a yes or no outcome, such as Logo fixated or brand recalled; or a percent of time that piles up at zero, such as Brow Furrow.
How are the observations linked?
In a within subjects design every participant gives a value in every condition, so the values come in pairs or sets from one person.
In a between subjects design different people give the values.
The worked example is within subjects for the ads and the A O I's, and between subjects only for order (AB or BA).
The table applies the three facts to every row of the plan.
The iMotions article General Data Analysis and Interpretation offers a decision chart (figure below; Workshop 7 used it for H 3).

Walk Q 5 through it: the ad is a discrete independent variable with two conditions (" at most 2"), we are not comparing a sample to a population, and the conditions are not independent, because the same people saw both ads.
The chart ends at "Repeated measures t-test", the paired t test.
Q 4 , with three A O I's ("> 2") measured on the same people, ends at "Repeated measure A nova".
The chart is a start, not a plan.

It has no branch for rank based tests such as the Wilcoxon signed rank test, none for yes or no outcomes, no effect sizes, and no linear mixed models, and it asks only about the independent variables, never what kind of number the outcome is: the question that sends recall to McNemar and Brow Furrow to a rank based check.

Its "Mixed model A nova" box, for designs with at least one independent and one repeated factor, is not the linear mixed model of the plan but an analysis of variance with a between and a within subjects factor, the shape of the order check O 1.
Its last box on the continuous side is too small to read in the P D F (it appears to say "Kappa's alpha"); it is on the Items to verify list (section 11).
Every test assumes something, and the plan names a check for each assumption it cannot take for granted.
The paired t test, which works on each participant's difference between two conditions, assumes that the differences are roughly normal, or that the sample is large enough for that not to matter.

Percent of time piles up at zero, and you can know that before testing: Workshop 7 found no Joy at all in 11 of its 44 participant by ad observations (simulated), and Brow Furrow, which faces rarely show, was zero in both ads for 17 of 22 participants (section 08).
Most differences are then zero, and a t test rests on the few people who differ.

The plan therefore pairs every paired t test with a Wilcoxon signed rank test, which ranks the differences by size and drops the zeros; when the differences are far from normal, as a Shapiro Wilk test can show, the rank based test is the guide.
The linear mixed model of Q 4 assumes one spread of the errors for all three A O I's, yet dwell on a small Logo that many viewers never look at is likely to vary less than dwell on a large Product.

So the plan adds a repeated measures A nova, which tests each effect against its own error term, with the Greenhouse Geisser correction, which reduces the degrees of freedom when the differences between pairs of conditions do not vary equally, and paired follow ups that use each comparison's own spread.
Section 08 says what each check showed.
In plain words.
Two values from one person are not two people.
Some participants smile at everything, some sweat more, some like every ad.
A paired test removes those personal levels by working on each person's difference; a mixed model does the same with a random intercept, a personal starting level.
An independent samples t test, which assumes that every value comes from a different person, does neither.

The paired test in symbols t equals Md divided by (standard deviation of the differences divided by the square root of n), df equals n - 1; d z equals Md divided by standard deviation of the differences Md and standard deviation of the differences are the mean and standard deviation of the differences, one per participant.
The personal levels cancel in each difference; an independent test builds its error from the raw values, which keep them.
Md and standard deviation of the differences are the mean and standard deviation of the differences, one per participant.
The personal levels cancel in each difference; an independent test builds its error from the raw values, which keep them.
Ignoring the pairing can go wrong in both directions.
Within one comparison it usually leaves the person to person spread in the error, so a real difference is harder to detect.

Pooling repeated observations as if they came from different people overstates precision: the Soft Drink sample report regresses liking on facial valence over 230 tastings from about 40 people, up to six each, as if they were 230 independent points (section 06 returns to it).
The plan's mixed models, fitted with L M E 4, give each participant a random intercept.
The same logic applies to the ads themselves.
The study has one ad per brand, so a difference between the ads cannot be separated from those two particular ads.
Treating ads as a random factor, a sample from all the ads a brand might run, takes several ads per brand (Judd and colleagues
, 2012), and in such designs power depends on the number of stimuli as well as the number of participants.
Section 10 turns this into advice for the next study.
In plain words.
Recall of each ad is yes or no, and each participant answered for both ads.
Sort the 22 participants by recall after Ad A and recall after Ad B.
People who recalled both brands, or neither, say nothing about which ad is remembered better; only the discordant pairs, people who recalled one brand but not the other, carry that information.
McNemar's test asks whether the discordant pairs split evenly; its exact version is a binomial test on them.

Recall was 12 of 22 for each ad.

McNemar or chi square?
A chi square test, or Fisher's exact test when counts are small, compares groups of different people.
When the same people answer twice, the 44 recall answers are not 44 independent observations, and a chi square test of ad by recall would treat them as if they were.
H 1 is a middle case: its pooled table of Logo fixated by recall holds two observations per person, which is why the plan adds each ad alone and a mixed logistic regression as checks.
Why.

The tests run outside iMotions, but every number they use was computed inside an iMotions analysis, a named selection of respondents, stimuli, and signal processing flows within a study, and every visual a client sees is drawn from one.

"Results are calculated over Annotations, according to the Signal Processing and/or A O I's included in your analysis" (Analysis Overview), so a comparison must exist in the analysis before it can exist in an export: an ad without A O I's has no dwell values, a time window that is not an annotation has no rows of its own, and a notebook never added has no metrics.
An annotation added after the notebooks ran needs the analysis recalculated (right-click the analysis, then Recalculate; Project doc 02b).

A segment is the group of respondents an analysis includes; segments are for seeing, not for testing.

The vendor's screenshots suggest one analysis per segment (Analysis, Analysis Expert, and Analysis Novice under one study), so showing a client the two order groups takes one analysis per value of Group.
Whether the Group list shows the values typed at the sessions, and whether one Aggregate Replay can show two segments at once, are items to verify.
The order test O 1 uses no segments: it models all 22 participants at once.

The worked example
Everything in sections 01 and 02 fits on one page.

Below is the simulated Multimodal Ad Study of Workshop 7 as the analysis sees it: the study in one paragraph for readers who skipped Workshop 7, the plan as a one page summary, the files, and what Workshop 8 adds.
Read it as a template for your own projects.
Everything about this study is simulated No person was recorded, no camera or sensor was switched on, and no file from a lab study was used.
A script wrote the Workshop 7 data (seed 20271231), and analysis full.
R computed every number in this workshop from them.
The participants are codes, P 01 to P 24; Altavo and Brenlow are invented brands; and the Altavo brand team is a fictional client.
Every number in this section is simulated, and no number in this workshop may be quoted as a finding.
The study in one paragraph.

Twenty-four participants came to the lab one at a time and saw, on the lab desktop, an instruction screen, a 60 seconds Baseline (a gray screen with a fixation cross), and two 30 seconds video ads for reusable water bottles: Ad A for Altavo, a hiking scene, and Ad B for Brenlow, a cycling scene.
Odd participants saw the ads in the order AB and even participants BA, and a survey slide followed.

A Smart Eye Aurora recorded gaze at 60 hertz on three A O I's per ad, Logo, Product, and Headline; Affectiva aff decks scored the face; and a Shimmer 3 G S R plus recorded skin conductance at 128 hertz.

Workshop 7 exported every file, applied three exclusion rules fixed before collection (R 1, use only recordings marked for use; R 2, exclude a participant whose eye tracking quality was below 90 percent or aff decks quality below 80 percent on an ad; R 3, drop a G S R value when less than 80 percent of its signal was present), merged the files into two analysis ready tables, and tested three hypotheses.
Rule R 2 removed P 18 and P 21, which left 22 participants, 11 in each order; rule R 3 removed the G S R value of P 05 for Ad B.
Which ad should we run?
The fictional Altavo brand team wants to know how its new hiking ad (Ad A) performs against a competitor's cycling ad (Ad B).
Section 01 translates the question into the plan below.
22 of 24 participants after rule R 2 (P 18 and P 21 excluded); 21 for G S R during Ad B after rule R 3; 66 participant by stimulus rows.
The order groups AB and BA hold 11 participants each.
Eye tracking: gaze dwell on the Logo, Product, and Headline as a percent of the ad, and whether the Logo was fixated (A O I export).
Face: percent of time with Joy, Engagement, and Brow Furrow at or above 50 (F E A export).
Arousal: G S R Peaks Per Minute during Baseline and each ad (G S R export).

Survey: liking of each ad (1 to 7), recall of each ad's brand (correct or not), attitude toward reusable water bottles (three items, 1 to 7), and purchase intention (one item, 1 to 7, asked once about reusable water bottles in general).
H 1, Logo fixation and brand recall: odds ratio equals 4.34, Fisher's exact p equals point 0 3 2.
H 2, Joy and liking: b equals 0.32 per 10 points of Joy, p equals point 1 1 0.
H 3, G S R Peaks Per Minute above Baseline: d z equals 0.83 for Ad A and 0.95 for Ad B, both Holm p less than point 0 0 1.
These must come out identical in Workshop 8.

Q 4 , attention by ad and A O I, with the follow ups Q 4 a (A O I's within each ad) and Q 4 b (each A O I between the ads); Q 5 , Joy, Engagement, and Brow Furrow by ad; Q 6 , the client's head to head comparisons on liking, recall, and arousal.
Written after collection, before these analyses ran.
O 1, order and position effects on liking and on dwell for each A O I: eight checks.
E1, 21 Spearman correlations among seven participant level measures, each with a 95 percent confidence interval and no p value.
P 1, the smallest effect 22 participants could detect, and the sample sizes the next study needs.
Two tailed tests at alpha equals point 0 5.
Holm's correction within each family: H 3 (2 tests), Q 4 a (6), Q 4 b (3), Q 5 (3), Q 6 (3), O 1 (8).
The omnibus tests of Q 4 are not adjusted.

step 1 of analysis full.

R reads the five Workshop 7 files, from the Workshop 7 folder when it is present and otherwise from ws7 inputs, compares the MD5 checksums of the two copies when both exist, and checks every column against the codebook.

step 4 then runs H 1 to H 3 again with the Workshop 7 code and compares the result with Workshop 7's output: all 55 printed lines are identical, and the 94 stored values differ by at most 1.9e-16, a relative difference at the limit of the computer's arithmetic.
This continuity check stops the script on any mismatch.
Why so strict?
If the same data and code gave a different answer in a second report, either the data or the code changed, and every result built on them would be in doubt.
A client who sees a number move between two reports without a stated reason stops trusting all of them.
Reproducing the earlier numbers exactly before adding new ones is the cheapest quality check a lab has.
Q 4 to Q 6 : where viewers looked in each ad, whether their faces differed between the ads, and the three comparisons the client asked for.
All are paired, because every participant saw both ads.
O 1: a check that the order of the ads did not decide the comparisons.
E1: how the measures of the four modalities go together across people, labeled exploratory.
P 1: what 22 participants could detect, and how many the next study needs.

Why.

The Aggregate Replay "replays the aggregated data from all respondents included in the analysis"; it is "the place where you review the sensor data of a group of respondents, typically with the purpose of spotting group-level patterns" (Aggregate Replay).
It exists only at the analysis level and shows exactly the respondents that the analysis includes: one analysis is one segment.
To compare groups, such as experts and novices, the vendor builds one analysis per group; whether one window can show two segments is an item to verify.
Select the analysis in the Library (section 02 shows how to create one).
You should see the analysis toolbar at the bottom of the main window.
Open the window.

Click a stimulus in the stimulus bar, click Aggregate, then the button that opens the window: "Edit Result" on screen in the release 8.1 article ("Edit result" in its text), "Open analysis" in the Analysis Overview and Heatmaps articles (Items to verify).
You should see the tabs Replay, Aggregate, and A O I, with Aggregate selected.
A gray Aggregate button means the window does not apply, as for "website recordings, face recordings, scene recordings and screen recordings".
Choose the panels from the "Panels" drop-down; here "the only available panels are the 'Stimulus', 'Signals', and 'Annotations' panels".
Common mistake.
Looking for a respondent: the aggregate window has no respondents and no faces, which is also why it can be shown to a client.

Effect sizes, intervals, and power: how big, how sure, and what 22 people could detect
The client asked one question: which ad should we run?
A p value cannot answer it alone.
It says how surprising a difference would be if the ads did not differ, not how large the difference is, how precisely it was measured, or whether 22 people could have revealed it.
Three tools answer those questions: the effect size (how big), the confidence interval (how sure), and the power analysis (what the study could have found).
Section 08 computes them for every question, and section 09 reports them.
Every number here is simulated, from analysis output dot T X T and simulated power dot C S V.
In plain words.
An effect size states a result on a scale that does not depend on how many people took part.

A p value shrinks as the sample grows even when the difference stays the same; an effect size does not, so effect sizes can be compared across studies and pooled, and the A P A task force on statistical inference asked for one beside every p value.
Give the raw difference too: 0.55 scale points of liking means more to a client than any standardized number.

Use the labels as a rough guide, and judge the size in the units that matter to the decision.
A 95 percent confidence interval is the range of values that the data are reasonably compatible with; its width shows how precisely the study measured the effect.
Read it in four steps (simulated values):
Width.
During Ad A, G S R peaks rose by 5.21 per minute over Baseline, 95 percent confidence interval 2.41 to 8.01: the true increase could be as small as about 2.4 or as large as about 8.0.
A wide interval means an imprecise estimate, whatever the p value.
Zero.
For a paired t test, a 95 percent interval of the mean difference that excludes 0 goes with p below point 0 5, and one that includes 0 with p of point 0 5 or more.
For an odds ratio, no effect is 1, not 0.
Both ends.
Liking was higher for Ad A by 0.55 scale points, 95 percent confidence interval -0.13 to 1.23.
The interval includes no difference and also an advantage of more than one full point; the data cannot tell these apart, which is not the same message as "the ads are liked equally."
What the 95 belongs to.
Over many repetitions, about 95 of 100 intervals made this way would contain the true value.
The 95 percent describes the method, not the probability that this one interval contains the truth (Greenland and colleagues
An effect size has an interval too: the script computes the interval of d z exactly from the noncentral t distribution; Excel's approximation can differ in the second decimal.
Client reports often give a number without its base or its interval.

The In-Store Shopper sample report gives each element of a display a time to first notice and " percent to Notice: 100 percent," but the page shows neither the number of shoppers (N equals 15 in its study details) nor an interval.
A percentage of 15 people is far less precise than the same percentage of 1,500, and only an interval shows how much less.
A p value starts from a model in which the effect is zero, the null hypothesis, plus every assumption of the test.
It is the probability, under that model, of a result at least as far from zero as the one observed.
A small p says that the data fit the model poorly, not which part of the model is wrong.

The General Data Analysis and Interpretation article calls it "the probability of observing the given results if the difference was due to chance only," a common shortcut: because p is computed by assuming that chance alone is at work, it cannot also be the probability that chance alone produced the result.
Four of the six principles in the American Statistical Association's statement on p values matter most for an ad test:
A p value does not measure the probability that a hypothesis is true, or that the data arose by chance alone.
Scientific conclusions and business decisions should not rest only on whether a p value passes a threshold such as point 0 5.
A p value does not measure the size or the importance of an effect.
Proper inference requires full reporting and transparency: every analysis run and every p value computed, not only the significant ones.
The most common misreading in client work turns "not significant" into "no difference."
For Joy (Q 5 ), d z equals 0.31, 95 percent confidence interval -0.12 to 0.74, Holm p equals point 3 3 1 (simulated): the interval includes no difference and also a moderate advantage for Ad A.
A nonsignificant result says that the data are compatible with no effect, not that the effect is absent.
The Soft Drink sample report titles a page "Emotional valence is a great predictor of liking" above a regression with Significance F 0.000094.
Try it: divide the regression sum of squares by the total, 40.98706 divided by 632.2609.
The result, R squared equals 0.065, means that valence accounts for about 6.5 percent of the variance in liking, a correlation of about point 2 5: a tiny p on a small effect.
The Total df of 229 adds a second problem.
The 230 tastings came from about 40 people (the report gives both 42 respondents and N equals 40) and are treated as independent observations, which overstates the precision and shrinks the p value.
A mixed model with a random intercept for each taster, as in H 2, is the remedy.

Each test at alpha equals point 0 5 accepts a 5 percent chance of a false positive when no difference exists, and the chances add up; in the words of the General Data Analysis and Interpretation article, "The more tests we conduct, the higher the chance of observing a false-positive result."
This analysis computes 38 tests with a p value, so the plan groups them into families, sets of tests that answer one question, and corrects within each.
The familywise error rate is the chance of at least one false positive in a family.
In plain words.
The Bonferroni correction multiplies every p by the number of tests, m.
Holm's correction sorts the p values, multiplies the smallest by m, the next by m - 1, and so on, and never lets an adjusted p fall below the one before it.
Both keep the familywise error rate at point 0 5; Holm is never less powerful.
The Bonferroni correction multiplies every p by the number of tests, m.
Holm's correction sorts the p values, multiplies the smallest by m, the next by m - 1, and so on, and never lets an adjusted p fall below the one before it.

Low power does double damage: true effects are missed, and the significant results that do appear tend to overstate the effect.
A sensitivity power analysis takes the sample actually tested and asks which effect it could have detected.

Joy (d z equals 0.31), Engagement (0.36), and liking (0.36) fall well below 0.63, and for d z equals 0.30 the power was point 2 7: about three studies in four of this size would miss a true difference that large, so "not significant" was the expected outcome.
The "N equals 30 per cell" of the iMotions TV and Digital Ad Testing template is a vendor convention, not a power calculation.
Why observed power is not used.
Some programs report observed power, the power computed for the effect the study happened to find.
It is a direct translation of the p value: a nonsignificant result always has low observed power, so it adds nothing and cannot show that a study was too small or that an effect is absent.
Plan power before a study, and report a sensitivity analysis after it.
A client who hears "we cannot tell" often asks whether the ads are then the same.
Only an equivalence test can say so.

It starts from the smallest effect size of interest, for example half a point of liking, agreed before the data exist, and runs two one sided tests, that the difference is above minus half a point and below plus half a point; if both are significant, the ads are equal for practical purposes.
This workshop names the test without computing it: no bound was set in advance, and the liking interval, reaching 1.23 points, is far too wide to succeed at half a point.

Paired data, paired lines.

A repeated measures A nova tests each effect against its own participant by effect error term, so it does not need the participant variance.
It assumes sphericity, that the differences between every pair of A O I's vary about equally across participants.

Reverse inference reads a mental state from a measure that can accompany it: the brow furrowed, so the viewer was confused.

The General Data Analysis and Interpretation article warns against it for brain imaging, "if a brain region is activated, we cannot infer the presence of a cognitive process just because that brain region is activated," and the logic holds for every signal in this lab.
The inference is only as strong as the measure is specific to the state, and facial movements are not specific to emotions.

The power analysis turns the limitations into targets (simulated):
Participants.

At least 34 to detect a moderate difference (d z equals 0.50) on one paired measure with 80 percent power, 45 if three measures form a Holm family; 90 and 120 for a small difference (d z equals 0.30).
About 72 independent observations, with the number of people planned from one ad per person or a simulation of the mixed model, not by halving N.
Several ads per brand, so that the brand can be separated from the execution; when ads are a random factor, adding ads, not only people, is what raises power.
Purchase intention for each brand, asked after each ad and naming the brand.
A preregistration of every question, test, and correction before collection, so that questions like Q 4 to Q 6 carry full confirmatory weight.
The smallest difference that matters, agreed with the client in advance (for example half a point of liking), so that a null result can be tested for equivalence.
A client who paid for a study hopes for a winner, and the pressure to deliver one is real.
The analysis plan is the protection: written before the numbers existed, it names every test that must be reported.
Four rules follow.
Report every planned test, including every comparison of the two ads, none of which found a difference.

Never present an exploratory pattern, or a hypothesis made up after seeing the results, as if it had been predicted; undisclosed choices made after seeing the data can make almost anything significant.
Never let a heatmap, a ranking, or a bar of means stand in for a test.
And never sell a measure for more than it measures: a G S R peak indexes arousal, not liking.
As the A S A statement puts it, business decisions should not rest only on whether a p value passes a threshold.
The honest sentence, "we cannot tell which ad performs better," protects the client from paying for a difference that may not exist.
